chapters.1: After Moses' death, God commissions Joshua to lead Israel into the promised land, promising to be with him as he was with Moses. God repeatedly tells Joshua to be strong and courageous and to follow the law closely, and Joshua in turn instructs the people and the eastern tribes to prepare to cross the Jordan.
chapters.2: Joshua sends two spies into Jericho, where they are sheltered by a woman named Rahab who hides them from the king's men on her roof. Rahab, convinced that God has given Israel the land, asks the spies to spare her family when the city falls, and they agree, telling her to mark her house with a scarlet cord.
chapters.3: Israel prepares to cross the Jordan River behind the priests carrying the ark of the covenant. As soon as the priests' feet touch the water, the river stops flowing upstream, and the entire nation crosses on dry ground, confirming God's presence with Joshua just as he had been with Moses.
chapters.4: After crossing the Jordan, Joshua has twelve men take twelve stones from the riverbed and set them up as a memorial so future generations will remember how God stopped the water for Israel's crossing. The people cross safely, and Joshua also sets up stones in the middle of the Jordan itself.
chapters.5: Israel's males born in the wilderness are circumcised at Gilgal, restoring the covenant sign that had lapsed during the wandering years, and the nation then keeps the Passover. The manna stops once they begin eating the land's produce, and Joshua encounters the "captain of the LORD's host," who tells him to remove his sandals on holy ground.
chapters.6: Following God's unusual battle plan, Israel marches around Jericho once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day with priests blowing trumpets, after which the walls collapse and Israel takes the city. Rahab and her family are spared as promised, while the rest of Jericho's people and goods are destroyed, except for silver, gold, and valuables devoted to the Lord's treasury.
chapters.7: Israel suffers defeat at the small city of Ai after a man named Achan secretly keeps some of the forbidden plunder from Jericho instead of destroying or devoting it. Joshua discovers through lots that Achan is responsible, and Achan and his family are executed and his stolen goods destroyed, removing the guilt from the nation.
chapters.8: With the sin dealt with, God gives Joshua a plan to defeat Ai using an ambush: Israel pretends to flee, drawing the defenders out of the city, while a hidden force captures and burns it. Afterward, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and has the law of Moses read aloud to the entire assembled nation.
chapters.9: Hearing of Israel's victories, the Gibeonites trick Joshua into a peace treaty by disguising themselves as travelers from a distant land. When the deception is discovered, Israel honors the oath they swore but makes the Gibeonites permanent servants, assigned to woodcutting and water-carrying for the community and the altar.
chapters.10: Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel, so Joshua comes to Gibeon's defense; God sends hailstones on the enemy and, in response to Joshua's prayer, makes the sun and moon stand still so Israel can finish the battle in daylight. Joshua then captures and executes the five kings and conquers several southern Canaanite cities.
chapters.11: A coalition of northern kings led by Jabin of Hazor gathers a large army with many horses and chariots to fight Israel, but God again gives Israel the victory at the waters of Merom. Joshua goes on to defeat the remaining Canaanite kings throughout the land, and the chapter summarizes that Joshua took the whole land as God had commanded Moses.
chapters.12: This chapter is a summary list of the kings Israel defeated, first the two kings Moses conquered east of the Jordan (Sihon and Og) and then the long list of Canaanite kings Joshua conquered west of the Jordan. It functions as a record confirming the completeness of Israel's early conquests under both leaders.
chapters.13: With Joshua now old, God tells him there is still land to be allocated even though not all of it has been fully conquered, listing territories like Philistia and Geshur still to be divided by lot. The chapter then describes the territory already given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh east of the Jordan, as Moses had assigned.
chapters.14: The land west of the Jordan begins to be distributed by lot among nine and a half tribes, with the Levites receiving no territory of their own. Caleb, one of the original twelve spies who remained faithful, is specially rewarded with the city of Hebron because of his courage and loyalty to God decades earlier.
chapters.15: This chapter details the extensive boundaries and list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, Israel's largest tribal allotment. It also recounts how Caleb's daughter Achsah is given in marriage to Othniel after he captures a city, and Achsah secures an additional gift of springs from her father.
chapters.16: The descendants of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, receive their territorial allotment, and this chapter describes the boundaries given specifically to the tribe of Ephraim. It notes that the Ephraimites did not fully drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, allowing them to remain as forced laborers instead.
chapters.17: The other half of Manasseh's territory is described, including a special provision allowing the daughters of Zelophehad to inherit land since their father had no sons. The chapter also notes that Manasseh, like Ephraim, struggled to fully dislodge the Canaanites from some of its allotted cities.
chapters.18: At Shiloh, where the tabernacle is now set up, Joshua presses the seven tribes that have not yet received land to send surveyors so the remaining territory can be divided by lot. This chapter then describes the boundaries given to the tribe of Benjamin.
chapters.19: This chapter records the land allotments for the remaining tribes: Simeon (within Judah's territory), Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, each listed with their cities and borders. It closes by noting that Joshua himself is given the city of Timnathserah as his personal inheritance.
chapters.20: Following earlier instructions from Moses, Israel formally sets apart six cities of refuge across the land where someone who kills another person accidentally can flee for protection from revenge until given a fair hearing. These cities ensure a measure of justice and safety is built into the nation's legal system.
chapters.21: The Levites, who received no land of their own, are given cities with surrounding pasturelands out of the other tribes' territories, fulfilling God's earlier command through Moses. The chapter closes by affirming that God had given Israel rest and fulfilled every promise he had made to their ancestors regarding the land.
chapters.22: With the conquest largely complete, Joshua commends and sends home the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh to their land east of the Jordan, urging them to remain faithful to God. A dispute arises when the western tribes fear the eastern tribes' newly built altar signals rebellion, but it's resolved peacefully once they explain it is only a memorial of their shared faith.
chapters.23: Now elderly, Joshua gathers Israel's leaders for a farewell address similar to Moses', reminding them that God fought for them and urging them to remain faithful, avoid intermarriage with remaining Canaanites, and not worship other gods. He warns that disobedience will bring the same kind of disaster on them that overtook the nations they displaced.
chapters.24: Joshua assembles the people at Shechem and recounts Israel's whole history from Abraham through the conquest, highlighting God's faithfulness at every step. He challenges the people to choose whom they will serve, and they commit to serving the Lord; the book closes with Joshua's death and burial, along with notes on Joseph's bones and Eleazar's death.
